newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Germany stands firm on EMU's slippery slope.
newsitem.headline: Germany stands firm on EMU's slippery slope.

text.p: Germany's uncomprising stance on a budget stability pact for those joining European monetary union reflects a deep-seated wariness over a bureacratic process with too many potential loopholes.

At a meeting of the European Union's monetary committee on Tuesday, there was once again little progress on resolving several outstanding details of a pact designed to penalise governments running excessive deficits.

While there is still a chance the group -- made up of EU finance and central bank officials -- can strike a deal when they meet again next week, the prognosis of some officials is that work on the pact will continue into next year.

The primary obstacle is Germany and its demands for a much tougher accord. Officials say Bonn's intransigence stems from several sources, but some argue it can be summed up in two very fundamental ways.

First, after a relatively successful meeting of EU finance ministers and central bankers in Dublin in September, Germany came away believing that a budget stability pact would indeed have a high degree of automaticity -- quick imposition of fines -- which would dissuade governments from profligate spending.
From a legal standpoint, the language contained in the draft examined in Dublin was considered vastly superior to that in the EU's current excessive deficit procedure.
Yet when the time came for the European Commission to put its own fingerprints on the blueprint in October, the result was considered by Germany to be a great step backwards.
"The Commission's draft was seen as a weaker version of the language contained in the initial (Monetary Committee) draft," said one EU official.

In particular, wording that suggested the "presumption" of sanctions being imposed on governments was altered to a "rule", which in EU legal terms offers more room for avoidance. "Where there is a rule there is an exception," was the way one official described the change.

As a result, Germany felt compelled to offset the renewed weakness by arguing for points that it initially wanted: a precise definition of exceptional economic circumstances and no ceiling on the level of fines, for example.

Under the current proposal, a country could escape sanctions if it suffered a severe economic downturn. The Commission was forced to avoid quantifying the extent of such a business contraction due to strong objections from several commissioners.
But given the overall weakness of the pact, Germany now wants a recession defined as a GDP fall of 2.0 percent.
What has emerged so far is the idea of a negative growth range -- between 0.5 percent and 2.0 percent GDP. Officials say it is unclear whether the proposal will mollify Germany.

A second aspect to Germany's hardline stance is the Bundesbank whose president, Hans Tietmeyer, had wanted the stability pact to be streamlined in a way that is completely contrary to the current process.

Instead of having a qualified majority of EU finance ministers vote on whether to take the procedure each additional step -- say from identification of an excessive deficit to a country having to place an initial deposit with the EU -- Tietmeyer wanted the voting process reversed -- a majority would be needed to block each step along the way to eventual fines.
"The Bundesbank appears to be an important factor behind the tough stance," said another EU official.

Apart from the specifics of the budget accord there is growing German nervousness over creative accounting by governments and the perception in financial markets that politics, not economics, is what counts in the EMU convergence process.

The latest wrinkle in this saga is Italy's "euro tax" proposal for its 1997 budget, considered by many as a blatant one-off measure. The tax has already raised eyebrows in Brussels and might be subject to a thorough review by Eurostat, the EU's statistical office.
